title: Checking a response and recording what actually happened
provenance: Original fictional practice commissioned for this curriculum; not authentic IELTS, not standardised or score-calibrated. No third-party text or diagrams used.
license: CC BY 4.0 for original text and SVG; no audio rights or audio files supplied.
word_count_method: Regex word tokens including hyphenated forms; excludes speaker labels, titles, question text and Q locators.

planning_only.note: Text-based estimate only. Future rendition must fit 32 minutes including part pauses; if not, revise the timetable before release.

tasks.task: Future continuous first listen, including planned part pauses
Submit first answers and confidence, without a second play
Four Q-located intensive segments, 15 minutes each

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Learning centre, how can I help?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Our group wants to practise entering and checking answers. We found a course called keyboard skills, but we can already type ordinary messages.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Interface practice is the more suitable workshop.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Please record interface practice as our choice. We want to understand how a checking routine works when the page layout changes.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: The session uses a fictional local exercise. It can help you record actions and notice mistakes, but it isn't access to a real examination interface.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Then attendance won't prove that we've operated the system used for a particular examination.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Correct. That would need a separate, genuinely completed activity and an identifiable record.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Is the workshop on the tenth of April?

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: That was the provisional date. The confirmed session is on the seventeenth of April.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: The seventeenth suits us. I'll replace the earlier entry in our calendar.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: The confirmation will state the subject and date together.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I'll forward the complete message, because someone also saved information about the keyboard course.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Good. A date can look reliable when copied from another event, especially if both messages carry the same centre heading. Use the current booking record rather than assembling a new schedule from fragments of several notices that happen to look familiar.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: When does teaching begin?

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Ten fifteen in the morning. The centre opens at nine forty-five, but this workshop begins at ten fifteen.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: So nine forty-five is the opening time, not the lesson start.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Exactly. Arrive shortly before teaching to find your room.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I'll label the two times differently in our travel note.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: That helps. The introduction distinguishes a practice action from a verified completed action. If someone misses it, they might later mark a task complete merely because they saw the demonstration, even though they never entered or checked a response themselves under the stated conditions.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: How many places should I reserve?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Five people belong to our study group, but two cannot attend. We need three places.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Three are available.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: The absent members can read our notes, but we won't count them as participants.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: That's sensible. If attendance changes, reply to the confirmation before transferring a place.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I'll keep one current list.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: The practical activity uses pairs at some stages and individual responses at others. Knowing the number in advance lets the leader plan the arrangement without treating a person who only watched a demonstration as though they completed the same task as someone who used the practice controls.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: What is the total charge?

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Thirty-nine pounds for the three places altogether.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Thirty-nine for the whole booking, rather than for each person?

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Correct. The local practice materials are included. Access to any separate examination preparation service is not part of this booking.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I'll tell our treasurer both the total and the scope.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Please check those details on the confirmation before payment. If the amount or number of places differs, ask us to correct the record.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: We will. An unexplained difference should not be treated as an extra service that someone supposedly requested without telling the rest of the group.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Which document should we bring?

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Bring the task sheet from the exercise you want to discuss. We need its exact instructions, not only a list of corrected answers.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I'll bring the task sheet with its version label.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Keep any first response separate from the later correction. If you don't have an original response, the sheet is still useful for examining requirements, but it doesn't prove what you answered before feedback.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: So we shouldn't reconstruct a first attempt to make the folder look complete.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Exactly. A clear gap is better than a polished record that gives an invented sequence the appearance of something that actually happened.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Does the workshop use a real examination interface?

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: No. It uses our fictional local practice page. Any operation in a real interface must be arranged and recorded separately for the relevant format.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Then a screenshot of your page can't establish familiarity with the actual system.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Correct. Even if a control looks similar, its behaviour may differ. We aren't claiming that a particular examination saves, submits or displays answers in the same way.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: We'll keep those statuses separate.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: That distinction allows the workshop to be useful without attaching an unsupported claim to it. A checking routine can be practised locally while real interface experience remains unverified.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: May a participant watch first if the instructions are unfamiliar?

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Yes, if the leader agrees, but record that as observation rather than independent completion. Watching another person can clarify a procedure, yet it changes the information available before the participant's own attempt.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: So the later response should show that a demonstration preceded it.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Exactly. The record doesn't need to imply that observation is unhelpful. It needs to describe the activity accurately.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: We can use separate entries for watched demonstration and completed practice.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Good. Otherwise one tick beside a broad heading may hide several quite different experiences and make a later comparison difficult to interpret.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: One member needs instructions in a format that works with their reading application.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Please describe the practical requirement before the session. We can check what the local materials support and confirm any limits.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I won't assume a photograph of a printed page is equivalent.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Thank you. An agreed access arrangement should remain visible where it affects a comparison, but it doesn't automatically tell us whether the underlying checking routine worked.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: We should record the task and arrangement together.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Yes. That gives a later reviewer the conditions needed to interpret the response instead of forcing them to guess from the final answer alone.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: How should we report a booking change?

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Reply to the current confirmation with its reference. Public comments beneath the event notice do not update the attendance list. The message also contains a contact number for an urgent issue.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I'll keep the whole confirmation until after the visit.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Good. It includes the entrance details and the document to bring.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I'll remind everyone that this is local practice, not a completed real-interface task.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: That's the right expectation. The workshop can improve how you check and record an action, while leaving a separate activity marked unverified until somebody has actually carried it out.

turns.speaker: Centre host
turns.text: Welcome to the practice centre. North is at the top of the diagram, and the entrance is on the southern edge. The court in the centre is the fixed landmark. Check-in is directly south of the court, on the entrance axis. It is not in either southern corner. Please report there before joining the group. The letters mark positions rather than the initials of their functions. If you visited for another course, use today's plan instead of following a remembered route. A room that looks familiar may now serve a different activity, and the current briefing is the relevant source for this workshop's arrangement.

turns.speaker: Centre host
turns.text: The demonstration room is in the north-west corner. It lies west of the northern central room and diagonally north-west of the court. An earlier notice placed the demonstration directly north, but today's activity uses the corner room. The leader will show a fictional practice page and describe what evidence each action leaves. A demonstration is not a record that every observer performed the action. Keep those two things distinct when completing your activity log. The example controls belong to this local exercise; their location and behaviour should not be copied into a claim about an examination system that the group has not actually opened or used.

turns.speaker: Centre host
turns.text: The individual practice room is directly east of the court, level with its centre. It is not the south-east room. Participants use it after the demonstration under the procedure stated by the leader. Preserve the first response before making corrections, and record any help received. If somebody points out a missing answer, the later corrected page should not be described as the untouched first attempt. Both versions can contribute to learning, but they answer different questions. The room arrangement supports separate work; it does not by itself prove that every response was unaided or that the task matches the conditions of a real examination.

turns.speaker: Centre host
turns.text: The review room is in the north-east corner. It is directly north of the practice room and directly east of the northern central room. Those northern spaces share a row, so the review room is east of its neighbour, not north-east of that neighbour. Groups meet there to compare a recorded action with the requirement it was intended to satisfy. A participant may remember clicking a control without knowing which response was sent. The review asks what the available record supports. It should not replace a missing confirmation with confidence or treat the intended action as evidence that the intended result necessarily occurred.

turns.speaker: Centre host
turns.text: The resource desk is in the south-west corner. It is west of check-in and below the room directly west of the court. Collect the worksheet version identified in the briefing. Some pages concern checking the content of an answer, while others concern recording the state of a local submission. Their tables look similar, but they ask different questions. If a sheet is missing, ask the helper rather than borrow a completed page from another participant. The desk supplies material; it does not verify that a real examination interface has been operated. That status depends on separate evidence from the actual activity, not on receiving a resource here.

turns.speaker: Centre host
turns.text: The first activity asks you to separate the task requirement from the mechanics of entering a response. A fluent typing performance can still produce an answer that repeats a unit or exceeds a word limit. Before using the local controls, identify what belongs in each blank and which information is already printed. Then examine whether the entered response satisfies that requirement. This is a content check, not proof of familiarity with another interface. Keeping those purposes separate helps you decide what a difficulty actually concerns. Otherwise a smooth interaction with the practice page may conceal a misunderstanding of the question, while a navigation error may be mistaken for lack of subject knowledge.

turns.speaker: Centre host
turns.text: During the exercise, preserve the position of a skipped item. A participant may move on deliberately rather than spend the whole period on one uncertainty. The record should make it possible to return to that item during the permitted checking stage of this local task. Do not assume that every other system provides the same mechanism. Follow the instructions for the actual activity being used. A general checking habit can be useful across settings, but the available controls and timing need separate verification. If a real interface has not been opened, its behaviour remains unknown, however confidently someone remembers a demonstration from another environment.

turns.speaker: Centre host
turns.text: When changing an answer, examine the resulting response rather than only the action you intended. A correction can affect spacing or another field if attention shifts between controls. The local task asks participants to compare the final visible entry with the requirement before recording it as checked. That observation is narrower than a claim that every change was safely stored or transmitted. The record should distinguish what was visible, what was sent and what confirmation was available. These are related stages, but one should not be used as a substitute for another merely because they usually occur close together during a familiar routine.

turns.speaker: Centre host
turns.text: If the local page behaves unexpectedly, stop the comparison and note what happened before making an explanatory claim. A delay could concern the practice setup, the network or the action sequence, and the visible result may not distinguish them. Ask the leader how the exercise should proceed. Do not mark a response successfully submitted solely because a control was pressed. The purpose is to learn how to preserve a usable account of an uncertain event. A careful record can include an unresolved status. Inventing a successful ending would remove the very evidence needed to investigate why the result differed from the participant's expectation.

turns.speaker: Centre host
turns.text: At the end, record the activity actually completed. Reading a checklist, observing a demonstration, entering a local response and operating a selected real interface are separate events. One does not automatically complete the others. If the real-interface task remains unperformed, leave that status unverified and identify what evidence would be needed later. The local exercise can still reveal a duplicated unit, a lost question position or an unclear checking sequence. Those observations are useful within their scope. The review should improve the connection between an action and its record, rather than turn a broad completion tick into evidence for experiences nobody has actually had.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: You compared the two local practice arrangements last week. What should the next trial use?

turns.speaker: Ken
turns.text: A keyboard-based version after the paper exercise. I want to see whether the checking routine survives the change in input.

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: I'd review the requirements on the existing sheets first. We still haven't separated entry errors from misunderstandings of the blank.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Ken, does that change your proposal?

turns.speaker: Ken
turns.text: It gives us something to record, but I still support the keyboard trial next.

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: I remain in favour of reviewing the current responses first.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Then Ken supports the new input trial, while Rosa wants another step before the group changes the arrangement.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Should you preserve the version actually submitted?

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: Yes. A corrected working copy isn't enough to show what was sent at the end of the attempt.

turns.speaker: Ken
turns.text: I agree. I initially thought the final file in the folder would identify it, but that file can be edited later.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: How will you distinguish the versions?

turns.speaker: Ken
turns.text: Use a clear label and retain the record linked to the local submission.

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: That will keep a later improvement from being mistaken for the original response.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Good. You both support preserving the submitted version, without treating its existence as proof that every other stage of the activity was completed correctly.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Rosa proposes reading the answer requirements aloud before the next trial.

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: I support that. Saying the instruction might reveal that somebody has overlooked a printed unit or word limit.

turns.speaker: Ken
turns.text: I'd use a short written summary instead. Reading aloud could become repetition without checking meaning.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Could a partner explain what they heard?

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: Yes, that is the version I favour.

turns.speaker: Ken
turns.text: It would help, but I still prefer the written summary for the next comparison.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Then Rosa supports the spoken check and Ken doesn't. You share the aim of clarifying requirements, but that doesn't make your preferred methods the same procedure.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Your first report marks real-interface practice complete after the local exercise.

turns.speaker: Ken
turns.text: I wrote that because the pages looked similar. I can see now that the entry isn't justified.

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: I don't support keeping it. We didn't use the real interface or verify its behaviour.

turns.speaker: Ken
turns.text: I'll remove the completion claim and record only the local task we actually performed.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Does either of you want to retain it with a question mark?

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: No. The separate activity should remain unperformed or unverified, not appear as a completed task with a minor caveat.

turns.speaker: Ken
turns.text: Agreed.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Then neither student supports the original completion claim.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Should the record describe actions rather than intentions?

turns.speaker: Ken
turns.text: Yes. Pressing a button, seeing an entry and receiving a confirmation are distinct observations.

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: I agree. We shouldn't write successfully submitted if the available evidence only shows that someone attempted to submit.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Would that make the record excessively cautious?

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: Not if we state the observed result precisely. An unresolved status is information, not an empty page.

turns.speaker: Ken
turns.text: It also tells us what another check would need to establish.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Then both of you support recording what happened, with uncertainty retained where the evidence doesn't settle the result of the intended action.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Ken suggests introducing a second page layout in the next trial.

turns.speaker: Ken
turns.text: I support it. We need to know whether participants recognise the checking task when familiar positions change.

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: I'd keep the current layout for one more attempt, so we can examine the revised instructions without adding another difference.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Could the second layout preserve the same questions?

turns.speaker: Ken
turns.text: Yes, and I still favour using it.

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: I understand the purpose, but I prefer to defer that change.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Then Ken supports the second layout and Rosa doesn't support it for the next trial. A useful future comparison isn't automatically the action both participants want to take immediately.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Which two checks are agreed for the preparation sheet?

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: Check every required output against the question instructions.

turns.speaker: Ken
turns.text: Agreed. A response can look complete while omitting a required item or repeating information supplied in the prompt.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Are you selecting typing speed as the main criterion?

turns.speaker: Ken
turns.text: No. Speed doesn't tell us whether the entered answer satisfies the requirement.

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: We also don't need a prediction of an official score.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Then required-output checking is one selected action. It concerns the work the participant must supply, not a general impression that the page looks full or that the input process appeared smooth to an observer.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: What is the second agreed check?

turns.speaker: Ken
turns.text: Record the state of the local submission, including the evidence available for that state.

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: Yes. We need to distinguish an attempted action from a response that the local record identifies as received.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Does that establish the behaviour of a real examination system?

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: No. The statement stays attached to this local exercise.

turns.speaker: Ken
turns.text: And it doesn't require a decorative chart or a ranking of participants.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Good. The selected pair is checking required outputs and recording submission state. Keep those two checks separate so that a success in one isn't used to conceal an unresolved result in the other.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: What limits the comparison from last week?

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: Participants knew the questions in the second arrangement because they had already seen them on paper.

turns.speaker: Ken
turns.text: That familiarity could reduce errors independently of the interface change.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Were the response pages missing?

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: No. Both sets were saved. The limitation concerns prior exposure, not lost records.

turns.speaker: Ken
turns.text: We can still examine entry behaviour, but we shouldn't claim the higher total came entirely from the new layout.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: State what was familiar and how the order was arranged. A clear description lets a later reviewer see which comparison was actually made instead of assuming two equally unfamiliar first attempts.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Was assistance equal?

turns.speaker: Ken
turns.text: No. An observer gave a hint about a skipped item during one attempt.

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: The note records the hint, so we can keep it visible when discussing the eventual answer.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Does that make the attempt useless?

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: No, but it narrows what we can say about independent checking.

turns.speaker: Ken
turns.text: Neither session was cancelled and the materials were available.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Then prior familiarity and the unequal hint are the two limitations to retain. Don't replace them with a generic list of possible technical problems that didn't occur. The review should explain this comparison rather than supply a collection of reasons any trial might have been imperfect.

parts.title: From a requirement to a recorded submission

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: Consider a fictional team reviewing an answer-entry procedure. The first stage identifies the requirement governing the response. This stated requirement may concern the requested information, the permitted length or a unit already printed around the blank. The team examines it before discussing how quickly an answer was entered. A smooth sequence of actions can produce a response that fails the task. The requirement should remain connected to the question version used in the attempt, since a later instruction may ask for something different. This stage establishes what the response must satisfy; it does not establish how a real examination interface behaves or prove that an unfamiliar system has been operated.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: The second stage prepares a working draft. The draft is the response under construction, before the final checking and submission stages of this local exercise. Keeping that distinction visible allows a participant to revise without pretending that every version was the answer eventually sent. The team should not infer which draft was final merely from the order in which files appear in a folder. A clear version label and an event record provide a better basis. The purpose is to preserve the relationship between the work being developed and the task it is meant to answer, rather than create a misleadingly tidy history after the outcome is known.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: The third stage completes validation against the instructions. Validation is a check of whether the entered response meets the stated requirements. It includes inspecting the actual words, numbers and units, not simply recalling what the participant intended to type. This validation check belongs to the local procedure being examined. It should not be described as a guarantee that another system stored or received the same content. If the visible entry differs from the intended answer, the team records the difference and the subsequent correction separately. The value of validation lies in connecting the response with a requirement that can be inspected, rather than relying only on the confidence of the person who entered it.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: The fourth stage saves the submission that was actually sent. Here, the submission means the submitted response, rather than every draft that preceded it. This sent version must remain identifiable after later corrections are made for learning. Without that distinction, a reviewer may compare the result with a cleaner response that did not exist at the time of sending. The record should also state what evidence identifies the submitted response. A participant's intention may be relevant, but it isn't interchangeable with an observable record. Keeping the version clear allows the team to examine both the original result and the improvement without silently replacing one with the other.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: The fifth stage records the status of the local submission. The status must reflect the evidence available, such as a local record that indicates receipt or an unresolved result after an attempted action. This recorded status should not become successful merely because the participant expected success. Nor should a local confirmation be treated as evidence about the behaviour of a different system. The team states what the observation establishes and what remains unknown. A carefully limited status supports a useful next check, while an invented completion entry removes the distinction between what happened, what was intended and what still needs to be verified in the relevant environment.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: The named practice of keeping identifiable versions in a clear sequence is version control. In this example, version control helps the team distinguish a working draft, a submitted response and a later correction. It does not require a complicated tool; it requires labels and relationships that another reviewer can follow. A filename such as final can become ambiguous when another edit is saved over it. The team should preserve the relevant object rather than rely on the label alone. The term names the management of versions, not a score for answer quality or evidence that every action associated with a file was successfully completed.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: An interruption can also cause a participant to lose their position in the task. The current position should be recoverable from the practice record without inventing an answer to fill the gap. This is the place at which the participant needs to resume, not necessarily the last item visible on the screen after someone else interacts with it. The team should record any relevant action during the interruption. A later return can then be understood in relation to the actual sequence. Preserving position supports continuity, but the available mechanism must be checked in the environment being used rather than assumed from another page that happens to look similar.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: A signal showing a system's response to an action is called feedback in this discussion. System feedback may indicate that an entry changed, that a local request was received or that an action needs attention. The meaning depends on the particular signal and environment. The team should describe what was observed instead of treating every visual change as a confirmation of success. This use of feedback concerns the system response, not a teacher's judgement of whether the answer was correct. Keeping those meanings distinct helps the review avoid an inference that a response was academically sound merely because the local page reacted after it was entered.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: The lecture uses the term side effect for an unintended change to another response during an action. For example, correcting one entry may leave another altered if the participant's attention moves to a different field. This is a fictional illustration, not a claim about a particular examination system. The team examines the resulting record and the sequence that produced it before deciding how to prevent a recurrence. A side effect can be small and still matter if it changes the submitted content. The named concept identifies an unintended consequence of an action; it should not be used as a general label for every wrong answer or every unexplained delay in an exercise.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: Finally, auditability names the property of a record that allows another reviewer to inspect the basis of its claims. An auditable record connects the task version, response, relevant actions and observed result. It also preserves an unknown status when the evidence does not settle a question. Auditability does not mean that the record proves every desired conclusion. It means a reviewer can see what supports the stated conclusion and where its limits lie. The local exercise ends with a record of what was practised and what remains unverified. Actual operation in a selected real examination interface is a separate event, and its completion must not be invented from this fictional rehearsal.
